question: Which nerve carries the motor supply to the four muscles of mastication?
explanation: The muscles of mastication come from the first pharyngeal arch and are supplied by motor branches of the mandibular division (V3). The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression.

question: Which fibers of the temporalis muscle retract the mandible?
optionC: The deep fibers of the masseter
optionD: The inferior head of the lateral pterygoid
explanation: The nearly horizontal posterior fibers of the temporalis pull the condyle back; the anterior fibers elevate the mandible. The lateral pterygoid protrudes the jaw rather than retracting it.

question: Which major salivary gland produces an almost purely serous secretion?
explanation: The parotid has serous acini only. The submandibular gland is mixed, mostly serous, the sublingual is mixed, mostly mucous, and palatal minor glands are mucous.

question: The parotid (Stensen) duct opens into the mouth opposite which tooth?
explanation: The duct pierces the buccinator and opens at the parotid papilla on the buccal mucosa next to the maxillary second molar.

question: In health, the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint is made of:
optionB: Hyaline cartilage, as in other joints
explanation: The central disc is avascular, non-innervated dense fibrous connective tissue; only its posterior attachment (retrodiscal tissue) is vascular and innervated.

question: Why can enamel not repair itself once a tooth has erupted?
explanation: Ameloblasts form the reduced enamel epithelium and are lost when the tooth erupts, so mature enamel has no cells to lay down new matrix. Dentin can form reparative dentin because odontoblasts remain.

question: What is the main role of Hertwig's epithelial root sheath?
optionA: Laying down enamel on the crown
explanation: The root sheath maps out the number and shape of roots and induces odontoblasts to form root dentin. Its remnants persist as the epithelial rests of Malassez.

question: A second mesiobuccal canal (MB2) is most often found in which tooth?
explanation: The mesiobuccal root of the maxillary first molar is broad buccolingually and very often holds a second canal, which is a common cause of missed anatomy in endodontic treatment.

question: Which permanent tooth has the longest root?
explanation: The maxillary canine has the longest root in the dentition, which is why it is a strong abutment and a key cornerstone of the arch.

question: Which primary tooth's crown most closely resembles the permanent mandibular first molar?
explanation: The primary mandibular second molar has three buccal cusps like the permanent mandibular first molar behind it. The primary mandibular first molar has a unique shape with a prominent mesial cervical ridge.

question: Type 1 diabetes mellitus results from loss of which cells?
optionA: Alpha cells of the pancreatic islets
optionB: Delta cells of the pancreatic islets
optionC: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets
optionD: Acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas
explanation: Autoimmune destruction of the insulin-secreting beta cells causes type 1 diabetes. Alpha cells make glucagon and delta cells make somatostatin.

question: Local anesthetics stop nerve conduction by:
optionB: Opening calcium channels in the axon
explanation: The uncharged base crosses the nerve membrane and the charged form binds inside the sodium channel, so the action potential cannot rise and is not propagated.

question: Which type of collagen makes up most of the organic matrix of dentin and bone?
explanation: Type I collagen forms the mineralized matrix of bone, dentin and cementum. Type II is in cartilage, type III in reticular tissue and type IV in basement membranes.

question: Biological hydroxyapatite in enamel and bone is built mainly from which ions?
explanation: Hydroxyapatite is a calcium phosphate crystal, Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2. Fluoride can replace the hydroxyl to form the more acid-resistant fluorapatite.

question: Parathyroid hormone raises serum calcium mainly by:
explanation: PTH acts through osteoblasts (RANKL) to increase osteoclastic resorption, increases renal calcium reabsorption and activates vitamin D. Calcitonin lowers serum calcium.

question: Which artery supplies the pulps of the mandibular teeth?
explanation: The inferior alveolar artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, runs in the mandibular canal and sends dental branches to the mandibular teeth.

question: Which nerve supplies the palatal mucosa next to the maxillary premolars?
explanation: The greater palatine nerve supplies the hard palate mucosa from the molars forward to the canine. The nasopalatine nerve covers the area behind the incisors, and the lesser palatine nerve the soft palate.

question: Case: 45-year-old man. Two days after removal of an impacted tooth 32, his lower lip and chin on the right are numb, but his tongue feels normal. Which nerve is most likely injured?
explanation: Numbness of the lip and chin follows the mental nerve, the end branch of the inferior alveolar nerve, which runs close to the roots of mandibular third molars. Lingual nerve injury would numb the tongue.

question: Case: 70-year-old woman after surgery on the right side of her neck. When she sticks out her tongue, it deviates to the right, and the right side of the tongue is wasting. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: With a lower motor neuron hypoglossal lesion the genioglossus on the weak side cannot push, so the tongue points toward the side of the lesion.

question: Case: 33-year-old woman. Minutes after an inferior alveolar block she cannot close her right eye or raise her right eyebrow. What happened?
optionC: The buccal branch of V3 was blocked
explanation: A needle placed too far posterior can deposit solution in the parotid gland, where the facial nerve branches run. The palsy is temporary; the eye is protected until blinking returns.

question: Case: 28-year-old man. A swelling under the left side of his jaw grows painfully at meals and shrinks between them. Which gland most often holds such a stone?
explanation: Most salivary stones form in the submandibular gland, whose mucous-rich, alkaline saliva flows uphill through a long duct. Swelling at mealtimes is the classic sign of an obstructed duct.

question: Which epithelium covers the attached gingiva?
explanation: Attached gingiva and the hard palate are masticatory mucosa with keratinized (ortho- or parakeratinized) stratified squamous epithelium, which resists friction from chewing.

question: Which vitamin is needed for the intestine to absorb dietary calcium?
explanation: Active vitamin D (calcitriol) increases calcium absorption from the gut. A deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

question: Which primary tooth usually erupts first?
explanation: Mandibular central incisors usually appear first, at about 6 to 10 months, followed by the maxillary central incisors.

question: Compared with hydroxyapatite, fluorapatite begins to dissolve at:
explanation: Fluoride makes the crystal more stable, so fluorapatite resists acid down to roughly pH 4.5, below the critical pH of about 5.5 for hydroxyapatite.

question: Repeated self-induced vomiting erodes which tooth surfaces first?
explanation: Gastric acid is pushed forward by the tongue over the palatal surfaces of the upper anterior teeth (perimylolysis). The tongue protects the lingual surfaces of the lower teeth.

question: What does the salivary protein statherin do?
optionD: Kills bacteria by lysing their walls
explanation: Saliva is supersaturated with calcium phosphate. Statherin and acidic proline-rich proteins stop crystals growing on tooth surfaces, while bicarbonate does the buffering and amylase breaks down starch.

question: A diver feels sharp pain in a tooth with a leaking restoration while surfacing. This pressure-related tooth pain is called:
explanation: Barodontalgia is tooth pain from a change in ambient pressure, as in flying or diving, usually in a tooth with existing pulpal disease or trapped gas under a defective restoration.

question: A hard blow to the left mandibular body breaks the bone there. Which second fracture should be looked for?
explanation: Force on the mandibular body is carried around the arch to the weak opposite condylar neck, so a body or parasymphysis fracture is often paired with a contralateral subcondylar fracture.

question: Carbon monoxide poisoning harms tissues mainly because carbon monoxide:
optionA: Turns into carbonic acid in plasma
explanation: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with an affinity over 200 times that of oxygen and shifts the curve left, so less oxygen is carried and less is released to tissues.

question: Which change shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the right, releasing more oxygen?
explanation: Acidity, carbon dioxide, heat and 2,3-BPG lower hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen (the Bohr effect), which helps working tissues. The other changes shift the curve left.

question: Carpal tunnel syndrome in a dentist results from compression of which nerve?
explanation: The median nerve runs under the transverse carpal ligament; repetitive forceful pinch grips and bent wrists raise the pressure in the tunnel. The ulnar nerve is compressed in cubital tunnel syndrome.

question: Which operator posture lowers the risk of neck and shoulder disorders?
optionA: Upper arms close to the torso
explanation: A neutral posture keeps the upper arms relaxed at the sides, the neck nearly upright and the trunk untwisted. Magnification and patient positioning help keep it.

question: Notched, smooth lesions at the cervical facial area of several teeth in a patient who scrubs side to side with a hard brush are best described as:
explanation: Abrasion is wear by an external object such as a toothbrush and abrasive paste. Attrition is tooth-to-tooth wear and erosion is chemical loss from acid.

question: Case: 24-year-old man with a tongue barbell for 3 years. The lingual cusp of tooth 19 has cracked. What caused it?
explanation: Habitually clicking a barbell against the teeth delivers repeated impact loads that chip and crack cusps; tongue jewelry can also cause gingival recession on the lingual.

question: Case: 52-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease. Her mucosa is pale and her hemoglobin is 9 g/dL. What mainly causes her anemia?
explanation: Damaged kidneys make too little erythropoietin, so the marrow produces fewer red cells. Anemia of chronic kidney disease is usually normocytic.

question: Most of the x-ray photons produced in a dental tube come from which process?
explanation: Most photons arise as electrons slow down near tungsten nuclei, giving a continuous spectrum. Characteristic radiation is a small part of the beam, and Compton scatter happens in the patient, not the tube.

question: Raising the kVp while keeping other settings the same produces a beam with:
optionC: More photons at the same energy
explanation: Higher kVp gives more penetrating photons and a longer gray scale (lower contrast). Milliamperage changes the number of photons, not their energy.

question: Within the patient's tissues, which interaction of a diagnostic x-ray beam produces most of the scatter radiation?
explanation: In the diagnostic energy range, Compton interactions eject an outer electron and send a weaker photon off in a new direction, the main source of scatter. Photoelectric absorption removes the photon and gives image contrast; pair production needs far higher energies.

question: If the distance from the source to the receptor is doubled and nothing else changes, the beam intensity becomes:
explanation: By the inverse square law, intensity falls with the square of distance: twice the distance gives one over two squared, or one quarter.

question: Which phase of a low-copper dental amalgam is the weakest and least corrosion resistant?
explanation: The tin-mercury gamma 2 phase corrodes and weakens the set amalgam. High-copper alloys largely eliminate it by forming the copper-tin eta phase instead.

question: Which cavity preparation has the highest configuration factor (C-factor) for a bonded composite?
optionC: A Class II with one proximal box
optionD: A Class III with facial access
explanation: The C-factor is bonded walls divided by unbonded surfaces. A Class I box has five bonded walls and one free surface, so shrinkage stress is highest.

question: How does a light-cured resin-modified glass ionomer set?
explanation: Resin-modified glass ionomers keep the acid-base setting reaction of conventional glass ionomer and add a resin component that polymerizes with light (and often chemically), giving early strength.

question: Which all-ceramic material has the highest flexural strength for a posterior crown?
explanation: Monolithic yttria-stabilized zirconia is the strongest dental ceramic. Lithium disilicate is strong but less so, and feldspathic and leucite ceramics are weaker still.

question: How is the fitting surface of a lithium disilicate crown prepared for adhesive cementation?
explanation: Hydrofluoric acid dissolves the glass phase to create micromechanical retention and silane couples the ceramic to the resin. Zirconia, with no glass phase, is air-abraded and primed with MDP instead.

question: Which elastic impression material stays most dimensionally stable when the cast is poured days later?
explanation: Addition silicone sets with no by-product, so it changes little over time. Condensation silicone loses alcohol, polysulfide loses water and alginate loses or gains water within minutes.

question: What happens to set dental stone when more water is used in the mix?
explanation: Extra water leaves more porosity once it evaporates, so the cast is weaker. A thinner mix also sets more slowly and shows less setting expansion.

question: Erbium lasers can remove enamel and dentin because their wavelength is strongly absorbed by:
explanation: Erbium wavelengths are absorbed by water and hydroxyapatite, so the water in hard tissue vaporizes and ablates it. Diode and Nd:YAG wavelengths target pigment and hemoglobin in soft tissue.

question: On a panoramic image, why do structures far from the focal trough look blurred?
optionA: They lie outside the sharp layer
optionB: The beam is collimated too tightly
optionC: The exposure time is too short
explanation: A panoramic unit records a curved layer (the focal trough) sharply. Objects in front of or behind it are magnified, narrowed or blurred, which is why head position matters.

question: Case: 30-year-old man. On a periapical image of tooth 8 the tooth looks much longer than it is. What caused this?
explanation: With the bisecting technique, too little vertical angulation elongates the image and too much foreshortens it. Horizontal errors overlap the contacts.

question: Case: 52-year-old man who grinds heavily needs a crown on tooth 30 with little space between the arches. Which crown needs the least occlusal reduction?
explanation: Cast gold is strong in thin section, so it needs less occlusal reduction than ceramics or metal-ceramic crowns, which need room for porcelain thickness.

question: Case: 41-year-old woman with a Class V lesion at the gingival margin of tooth 6 that will be hard to keep dry. What is the main concern with placing a composite there?
optionB: The lesion is too shallow to restore
optionC: Composite cannot be shaded to match
explanation: Resin bonding is technique sensitive and fails with blood or saliva contamination, which is why isolation matters at cervical margins and why glass ionomer is often used there instead.

question: A radiograph shows thin enamel and dentin with large pulps, so the teeth look like ghosts in one quadrant. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Regional odontodysplasia affects enamel and dentin of a group of adjacent teeth, usually in one quadrant, so they look faint on radiographs. Amelogenesis and dentinogenesis imperfecta affect the whole dentition.

question: Which radiographic finding is typical of dentin dysplasia type I?
optionB: Short roots with crescent pulp remnants
optionD: Long roots with tall pulp chambers
explanation: Type I is the 'rootless teeth' form: short, blunt roots, obliterated pulps with a crescent-shaped remnant and periapical radiolucencies on teeth with normal-looking crowns.

question: Which hereditary condition affects the enamel while the dentin develops normally?
explanation: Amelogenesis imperfecta is a group of inherited enamel defects (hypoplastic, hypomaturation, hypocalcified) with normal dentin. The other conditions involve dentin.

question: Hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia most typically shows which dental finding?
optionD: Many missing teeth, conical in shape
explanation: Reduced sweat glands, sparse hair and hypodontia with peg or cone-shaped teeth are the classic triad; dentures or implants are often needed early.

question: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is recognized in the dental chair by:
optionD: Pits on the palms and soles
explanation: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome pairs perioral and oral melanotic macules with hamartomatous intestinal polyps and a higher cancer risk, so these patients should be under medical follow-up.

question: Nevoid basal cell carcinoma (Gorlin) syndrome is associated with which jaw lesions?
explanation: Multiple odontogenic keratocysts, often in young patients, should prompt a search for Gorlin syndrome: basal cell carcinomas, palmar pits and calcified falx cerebri.

question: In most people with Down syndrome, the extra chromosome results from:
explanation: About 95% of cases are full trisomy 21 from meiotic nondisjunction, usually maternal. Translocation and mosaic forms are much less common, and loss of an X chromosome causes Turner syndrome.

question: A cleft of the secondary palate results from failed fusion of which structures?
explanation: The secondary palate forms when the palatal shelves of the maxillary processes rise and fuse in the midline. A cleft lip involves the medial nasal and maxillary processes instead.

question: A permanent premolar erupts with a small, yellow, hypoplastic crown after its primary predecessor had an abscess. This is a:
explanation: Infection or trauma at a primary tooth can disturb ameloblasts of the developing successor, leaving a local enamel defect called a Turner tooth.

question: Notched, screwdriver-shaped permanent incisors suggest which congenital infection?
explanation: Treponema pallidum disturbs tooth formation, giving Hutchinson incisors and mulberry molars, part of Hutchinson's triad with interstitial keratitis and eighth nerve deafness.

question: Tetracycline can stain the permanent teeth when it is given during which period?
explanation: Tetracycline binds calcium in mineralizing teeth, so exposure while permanent crowns are calcifying, up to about age 8, can cause discoloration.

question: Dens invaginatus is most often found in which tooth?
explanation: The enamel organ folds into the crown most often in maxillary lateral incisors, leaving a pit that can let bacteria reach the pulp early; sealing the pit is often advised.

question: Taurodontism is a molar with:
optionC: An enamel pearl in the furcation
explanation: In taurodontism the body of the tooth is elongated and the furcation is displaced apically, giving a tall pulp chamber; it occurs alone or with syndromes such as Klinefelter.

question: A large anterior tooth with a notched incisal edge and one root canal sits in an arch with a normal tooth count. This is most likely:
explanation: Gemination is one tooth bud trying to divide, so the count is normal when the large tooth is counted once and there is usually one canal. Fusion joins two buds, so the count is one short.

question: Two adjacent maxillary molars are joined only by cementum. This is called:
explanation: Concrescence is union of roots by cementum after root formation, often from crowding or trauma. It matters before extraction, since removing one tooth may remove the other.

question: A primary molar sits below the occlusal plane and gives a dull sound when tapped. What is the likely cause?
explanation: Ankylosis fuses root to bone, so the tooth stops erupting while its neighbors keep growing, leaving it in infraocclusion; it has a solid, dull percussion note.

question: Hemophilia A is inherited in which pattern?
explanation: Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) is X-linked recessive, so it mainly affects males, and carrier mothers pass it to half of their sons.

question: Sickle cell disease results from which change in the beta-globin gene?
optionD: A frameshift in the beta gene
explanation: A single point mutation replaces glutamic acid with valine at position 6, so deoxygenated hemoglobin S polymerizes and red cells sickle.

question: Case: 3-year-old boy. Several primary incisors fell out with intact roots and no injury. His alkaline phosphatase is low. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Hypophosphatasia lowers tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, so cementum forms poorly and primary teeth, often incisors, exfoliate early with their roots intact.

question: Case: 10-year-old girl treated with chemotherapy at age 3. Her developing premolars and second molars have short, tapered roots. What is the likely cause?
explanation: Chemotherapy during early childhood damages cells forming the teeth, giving short V-shaped roots, microdontia or missing teeth depending on the stage reached.

question: Case: 11-year-old boy who can bring his shoulders together in front of his chest. Primary teeth are retained and radiographs show many unerupted extra teeth. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: A RUNX2 mutation causes absent or small clavicles, open fontanelles and many supernumerary unerupted teeth with retained primary teeth.

question: Case: 34-year-old woman with several hard swellings of the mandible and impacted teeth. Radiographs show multiple osteomas. Why is a medical referral urgent?
optionC: She is likely to have hemophilia
explanation: Multiple osteomas, impacted teeth and epidermoid cysts suggest Gardner syndrome, in which colorectal polyps carry a near-certain risk of cancer, so colonoscopy should not wait.

question: Case: 8-year-old girl with blue sclerae, several past fractures and opalescent, blue-gray teeth. Which condition explains her teeth?
explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a type I collagen disorder of bone, sclerae and often dentin, giving opalescent teeth like dentinogenesis imperfecta.

question: Case: 9-year-old boy whose permanent first molars and incisors have demarcated, chalky, yellow-brown enamel that breaks down easily. Other teeth are normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: MIH affects one or more first permanent molars, often with incisors, as sharply bordered opacities. Amelogenesis imperfecta affects all teeth, and fluorosis gives diffuse, symmetric mottling.

question: Which cells are the most effective at presenting antigen to naive T cells?
explanation: Dendritic cells, including Langerhans cells in oral epithelium, capture antigen, migrate to lymph nodes and activate naive T cells. Plasma cells secrete antibody and do not present antigen to naive T cells.

question: Plasma cells in an inflamed periodontal pocket wall develop from which cells?
explanation: Activated B cells differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibody. Plasma cells dominate the established lesion of chronic periodontitis.

question: Which antibody binds mast cells and triggers immediate (type I) hypersensitivity?
explanation: Allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine and other mediators within minutes, as in anaphylaxis and urticaria.

question: Serum sickness after an injected foreign protein is which type of hypersensitivity?
explanation: Antigen-antibody complexes deposit in vessels, joints and kidneys and activate complement, giving fever, rash and arthralgia about one to two weeks after exposure.

question: Which complement fragment is the main opsonin that coats bacteria for phagocytosis?
explanation: C3b on a bacterial surface binds complement receptors on phagocytes. C5a and C3a are anaphylatoxins (C5a is also strongly chemotactic), and C9 completes the membrane attack complex.

question: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency causes severe periodontitis in children because neutrophils:
optionD: Cannot present antigen to T cells
explanation: A defect in the CD18 integrin stops neutrophils sticking to endothelium and migrating out, so infections spread despite high blood neutrophil counts. Failure to make oxidants is chronic granulomatous disease.

question: Which molecule drives osteoclast formation and bone loss in periodontitis?
explanation: Inflammatory cytokines raise RANKL on osteoblasts and lymphocytes; RANKL binds RANK on osteoclast precursors. Osteoprotegerin is a decoy receptor that blocks it.

question: Oral lichen planus is best described as:
explanation: Cytotoxic T cells attack basal keratinocytes, giving a band of lymphocytes under the epithelium and degeneration of the basal layer.

question: In pemphigus vulgaris, autoantibodies are directed against:
explanation: Antibodies to desmogleins split the epithelium above the basal layer (acantholysis), so blisters rupture into erosions. Antibodies to hemidesmosomes cause pemphigoid, a subepithelial split.

question: HIV infects mainly which immune cells?
explanation: HIV uses CD4 with a chemokine coreceptor to enter helper T cells and macrophages. Falling CD4 counts lead to opportunistic infections and lesions.

question: After a full hepatitis B vaccine series, which blood marker shows immunity?
explanation: Vaccination produces antibody to the surface antigen only. HBsAg and HBeAg mark infection, and anti-HBc appears only after natural infection.

question: Which feature of inflammation is caused mainly by histamine making venules leaky?
explanation: Histamine from mast cells contracts endothelial cells in venules, so fluid and protein leak out and the tissue swells. Fever comes from cytokines such as IL-1 acting on the hypothalamus.

question: Case: 62-year-old woman with red, peeling gingiva and blisters that leave erosions. Biopsy shows a split below the epithelium. Her eyes are irritated. What referral is most important?
explanation: Mucous membrane pemphigoid often involves the conjunctiva, where scarring can lead to blindness, so eye assessment is needed even when the eyes look mild.

question: Case: 58-year-old man who started lisinopril last month has sudden swelling of the lips and tongue without hives. What causes this swelling?
explanation: ACE inhibitors stop the breakdown of bradykinin, which can cause angioedema without urticaria at any time during therapy. Antihistamines work poorly, and the airway is the first concern.

question: Case: 6-year-old girl with thick scaling skin on her palms and soles and severe bone loss around her primary teeth. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Loss-of-function mutations in cathepsin C impair neutrophil serine proteases, giving palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and aggressive periodontitis in both dentitions.

question: Case: 50-year-old man on chemotherapy with an absolute neutrophil count of 400 per cubic millimeter wants a routine scaling. What should the dentist do?
optionB: Proceed after a mouth rinse only
optionD: Defer it and consult the oncologist
explanation: An absolute neutrophil count under 500 is severe neutropenia with a high infection risk, so elective care waits for count recovery after discussion with the oncologist; urgent care is planned with the medical team.

question: Within the oral cavity proper, squamous cell carcinoma most often arises on the:
explanation: The lateral and ventral tongue and floor of the mouth are the high-risk sites for oral squamous cell carcinoma; the dorsum of the tongue is rarely involved.

question: Most HPV-positive oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinomas are linked to which type?
explanation: High-risk HPV 16 drives most HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancers, usually in the tonsils and base of tongue. Types 6 and 11 cause benign papillomas and warts.

question: Recurrent intraoral herpes simplex lesions in a healthy adult usually appear on:
explanation: Recurrent intraoral herpes favors keratinized mucosa bound to bone. Recurrent aphthous ulcers favor the nonkeratinized lining mucosa, which helps tell them apart.

question: Which odontogenic tumor typically appears as a multilocular, soap-bubble radiolucency in the posterior mandible of an adult?
explanation: Conventional ameloblastoma is locally aggressive, expands the posterior mandible and can resorb roots. Odontomas and cementoblastomas are radiopaque, and the adenomatoid tumor favors the anterior maxilla of teenagers.

question: A periapical (radicular) cyst is lined by epithelium that comes from the:
explanation: Inflammation from a necrotic pulp stimulates the rests of Malassez in the periodontal ligament. Rests of Serres give rise to gingival and lateral periodontal cysts, and reduced enamel epithelium to dentigerous cysts.

question: Which is the most common odontogenic tumor?
explanation: Odontomas, compound or complex, are hamartomas of enamel and dentin and are the most frequent odontogenic tumors, often found when they block eruption.

question: Which is the most common salivary gland neoplasm?
explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common salivary tumor, most often in the parotid. It is benign but recurs if shelled out without a margin.

question: Which feature makes adenoid cystic carcinoma especially dangerous?
optionB: It grows from a dentigerous cyst
explanation: Adenoid cystic carcinoma grows slowly but invades along nerve sheaths, causing pain or numbness and late recurrence or lung metastasis years after surgery.

question: A giant cell lesion of the jaw identical to central giant cell granuloma should prompt which test?
explanation: The brown tumor of hyperparathyroidism is histologically the same as central giant cell granuloma, so serum calcium, phosphate and PTH are checked before treatment.

question: Leukoplakia is defined as:
optionA: A white patch that wipes off
optionB: A white patch with no other diagnosis
optionD: A white lesion caused by tobacco only
explanation: Leukoplakia is a clinical term for a white plaque that cannot be characterized as another condition; it is a diagnosis of exclusion, and only a biopsy shows whether dysplasia is present.

question: A leukoplakia in which location carries the greatest risk of dysplasia or carcinoma?
explanation: White lesions of the floor of the mouth and ventral or lateral tongue are the most likely to show dysplasia or carcinoma when biopsied.

question: Which is the most common soft tissue mass in the mouth, usually on the buccal mucosa along the bite line?
explanation: Irritation fibroma is a reactive hyperplasia of fibrous connective tissue caused by chronic trauma such as cheek biting, and is treated by excision.

question: Replacement of one mature cell type by another, as in the airways of smokers, is called:
explanation: Metaplasia is adaptive replacement, such as columnar by squamous epithelium. Dysplasia is disordered growth with atypia, a step toward carcinoma.

question: Which type of necrosis follows a myocardial infarction?
explanation: Ischemia in solid organs except the brain preserves the tissue outline for a time (coagulative necrosis). The brain liquefies, tuberculosis caseates and pancreatitis causes fat necrosis.

question: Which condition calls for extra caution with epinephrine-containing local anesthetic?
explanation: In uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, added epinephrine can trigger tachyarrhythmias or a thyroid storm, so care waits for control or epinephrine is limited.

question: Under current guidance on preventing infective endocarditis, which history alone warrants antibiotic prophylaxis before gingival manipulation?
explanation: Prophylaxis is limited to the highest-risk conditions: prosthetic valves or valve repair material, prior endocarditis, some congenital heart disease and cardiac transplant with valvulopathy. Stents and pacemakers are not on the list.

question: Case: 55-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis needs two teeth extracted. Which laboratory tests matter most beforehand?
explanation: Liver disease lowers clotting factor production (a raised INR) and splenomegaly lowers platelets, both raising bleeding risk; many drugs metabolized by the liver also need dose changes.

question: Case: 46-year-old woman with bilateral parotid swelling, dry eyes and a dry mouth. Which complication must be watched for over the years?
explanation: Sjogren syndrome raises the risk of B-cell lymphoma, often MALT lymphoma in the parotid, so persistent or firm gland enlargement is investigated.

question: Case: 62-year-old smoker with a painless, firm ulcer 1.5 cm across on the lateral tongue that has lasted 5 weeks. What should be done?
optionD: Remove it by laser with no biopsy
explanation: An indurated ulcer that has not healed within two weeks of removing any likely cause needs a tissue diagnosis to rule out carcinoma, all the more in a high-risk site and patient; destroying it without a biopsy loses the diagnosis.

question: Case: 16-year-old boy with a slow, painless enlargement of the left maxilla. The radiograph shows a ground-glass pattern blending into normal bone. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Fibrous dysplasia replaces bone with fibrous tissue and woven bone, giving ill-defined ground-glass expansion that usually stabilizes after growth ends.

question: Case: 44-year-old man. A few weeks after a palatal injection, a painful ulcer appears on the hard palate. Biopsy shows necrotic minor salivary glands with squamous metaplasia. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Ischemic necrosis of palatal salivary glands mimics carcinoma clinically and microscopically but heals on its own in several weeks.

question: Case: 63-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on dialysis. Radiographs show loss of the lamina dura and ground-glass bone. What explains these findings?
explanation: Kidney failure lowers calcium and active vitamin D, so PTH rises and bone is resorbed, giving loss of lamina dura and sometimes brown tumors (renal osteodystrophy).

question: Case: 30-year-old woman. A small, painful, round ulcer with a yellow base and red halo appears on her labial mucosa a few times a year and heals in a week. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Minor aphthae are shallow, round ulcers under 1 cm on nonkeratinized mucosa that heal without scarring in 7 to 14 days. A chancre is usually painless and solitary.

question: Case: 67-year-old man with bone pain, anemia and several punched-out radiolucencies in the skull and mandible. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell disorder of older adults with bone pain, anemia, renal problems and sharply punched-out lytic lesions.

question: Which red complex organism produces gingipain proteases that degrade host proteins?
explanation: Porphyromonas gingivalis, with Tannerella forsythia and Treponema denticola, forms Socransky's red complex; its gingipains break down host proteins and disrupt immune signaling.

question: Fusobacterium nucleatum matters in dental plaque mainly because it:
optionA: Is the first colonizer of pellicle
explanation: Fusobacterium nucleatum coaggregates with early gram-positive colonizers and later gram-negative anaerobes, linking them as the biofilm matures.

question: Which genus increases as a caries lesion advances into dentin?
explanation: Lactobacilli are acid tolerant and thrive in the low pH of cavitated, dentinal lesions; they are linked more to progression than to the start of caries.

question: In invasive oral candidiasis, which form of Candida albicans penetrates the epithelium?
explanation: Yeast cells switch to hyphae that invade the superficial epithelium; hyphae on a smear or biopsy show active infection rather than simple carriage.

question: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease is most often caused by:
explanation: Coxsackievirus A16 and enterovirus 71 cause oral vesicles and ulcers with a rash on the hands and feet, mostly in young children.

question: Infectious mononucleosis, which can cause petechiae at the junction of the hard and soft palate, is caused by:
explanation: Epstein-Barr virus causes fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy and palatal petechiae, mostly in teens and young adults.

question: A worker is stuck by a needle used on a patient with hepatitis C. Which statement about follow-up is true?
optionA: A hepatitis C vaccine is given at once
optionC: No vaccine or proven prophylaxis exists
explanation: There is no hepatitis C vaccine and no recommended postexposure prophylaxis, so follow-up testing is done to find any infection early, when it can be treated. Hepatitis B, by contrast, has a vaccine and immune globulin.

question: Under CDC guidance, which sterilizer load must always be monitored with a biological indicator?
optionA: Every load of wrapped hand instruments
optionB: Only the first load after a holiday
optionC: Only loads run in a dry-heat unit
optionD: Any load with an implantable device
explanation: CDC guidance calls for at least weekly spore testing of each sterilizer and a biological indicator in every load that contains an implantable device, ideally held until the result is known.

question: Which organisms are usually cultured from an acute odontogenic abscess?
explanation: Odontogenic infections are polymicrobial, typically viridans streptococci with anaerobes such as Prevotella, Peptostreptococcus and Fusobacterium, which is why penicillin-class drugs are first choice when antibiotics are needed.

question: Sterilization differs from high-level disinfection because sterilization also kills:
explanation: High-level disinfection kills all microorganisms except high numbers of bacterial spores; sterilization destroys all microbial life, including spores.

question: Why do prions call for special handling of contaminated instruments?
optionA: They are killed by any disinfectant
optionD: They live only on plastic surfaces
explanation: Prions are misfolded proteins with no nucleic acid, so routine steam cycles may not inactivate them; special protocols or disposable instruments are used for known or suspected cases.

question: Endotoxin from gram-negative bacteria that stimulates inflammation in periodontitis is:
optionA: Teichoic acid of the cell wall
optionB: Peptidoglycan of the inner wall layer
explanation: Lipopolysaccharide in the outer membrane activates macrophages through toll-like receptor 4, driving cytokines that destroy tissue. Teichoic acid belongs to gram-positive walls.

question: Infection from the roots of a mandibular second molar that perforates the lingual plate below the mylohyoid line spreads first into the:
explanation: Mandibular molar roots lie below the mylohyoid attachment, so lingual spread enters the submandibular space; premolar and canine infections above the line enter the sublingual space.

question: Why can an infection of the upper lip spread to the cavernous sinus?
optionA: The lip drains to the jugular nodes
optionB: Its facial veins have no valves
optionC: The maxillary sinus opens into it
optionD: The lip lymph flows into the brain
explanation: The facial and angular veins connect with the ophthalmic veins and have no valves, so infected blood from the danger triangle can flow back toward the cavernous sinus.

question: A patient has a cough for 3 weeks, night sweats and weight loss, and suspected active tuberculosis. What should happen with elective dental care?
optionA: Treat with a surgical mask on
optionD: Treat at the end of the day
explanation: CDC guidance is to defer elective care for patients with suspected or confirmed active TB until a physician confirms they are not infectious; urgent care needs airborne precautions.

question: Primary syphilis in the mouth typically appears as:
optionB: A white plaque that wipes off
explanation: The chancre of primary syphilis is a painless, indurated ulcer at the site of inoculation, often with enlarged nodes, and is highly infectious.

question: Case: 38-year-old man, 3 weeks after an extraction, has a firm swelling at the angle of the jaw with draining sinuses that release yellow granules. What is the likely organism?
explanation: Cervicofacial actinomycosis forms slowly enlarging, woody swellings with draining sinuses and sulfur granules; it needs long courses of antibiotics, usually penicillin.

question: Case: 66-year-old woman with burning pain and vesicles on the left upper lip, palate and gingiva that stop sharply at the midline. Which virus is responsible?
explanation: Herpes zoster reactivates in one sensory ganglion, here the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, giving a unilateral band of vesicles that ends at the midline.

question: Case: 4-year-old with a fever, fiery red, swollen gingiva and many small ulcers on the lips and tongue for the first time. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: Primary HSV-1 infection in young children causes fever with generalized gingivitis and widespread vesicles that ulcerate. Herpangina is limited to the posterior soft palate and pharynx.

question: Case: 58-year-old man with diabetes and a firm, rising swelling of the floor of the mouth on both sides. He drools and his tongue is pushed up. What is the immediate priority?
explanation: Ludwig angina spreads through the submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces on both sides and can block the airway, so airway protection and emergency care come first.

question: Case: 72-year-old woman with cracked, red corners of the mouth under deep skin folds. Which organisms are usually involved?
explanation: Angular cheilitis is usually a mixed infection of Candida and Staphylococcus aureus, often helped by loss of vertical dimension that keeps the corners moist.

question: Case: 35-year-old woman with asthma who uses an inhaled corticosteroid has white plaques on her palate that wipe off. What advice prevents a recurrence?
optionB: Rinse with water after each puff
explanation: Inhaled steroids deposit in the mouth and suppress local immunity, allowing pseudomembranous candidiasis. Rinsing and spitting after each use, or a spacer, lowers the risk.

question: Case: 26-year-old man with fever, painful punched-out ulcers of the interdental papillae and a gray pseudomembrane. Which organisms predominate in the lesions?
explanation: Necrotizing periodontal diseases are dominated by spirochetes (Treponema) and fusiform bacteria with Prevotella intermedia, in hosts with stress, smoking or immune suppression.

question: Case: 40-year-old dental assistant cuts her finger on a used scaler. What is the first thing she should do?
optionC: Wait to report it at day's end
optionD: Wash it with soap and water
explanation: CDC guidance is to wash a percutaneous injury with soap and water at once, then report it so the source and exposure can be evaluated and postexposure care started quickly.

question: The articaine label gives a maximum dose of 7 mg/kg. What is the most a healthy 25 kg child may receive?
explanation: 7 mg/kg x 25 kg = 175 mg. At 40 mg/mL for 4% articaine, that is about 4.4 mL; 350 mg would be double the limit.

question: How many milligrams of epinephrine are in 1.8 mL of a 1:100,000 solution?
explanation: 1:100,000 means 1 g in 100,000 mL, or 0.01 mg/mL, so 1.8 mL x 0.01 mg/mL = 0.018 mg. A 1:200,000 solution would give 0.009 mg.

question: Which local anesthetic is most associated with methemoglobinemia when doses are high?
explanation: A metabolite of prilocaine (o-toluidine) oxidizes hemoglobin to methemoglobin, so it is avoided in patients with methemoglobinemia, G6PD deficiency or on other oxidizing drugs. Labels for other agents also carry the warning.

question: Which amide local anesthetic gives the longest soft tissue anesthesia, useful after oral surgery?
explanation: Bupivacaine is highly protein bound and lipid soluble, giving long duration that can control postoperative pain; it is not given to young children because of lip-biting risk.

question: Articaine is an amide, yet much of it is broken down in the blood. Why?
optionA: It has an ester side chain
optionC: It is cleared unchanged by the kidney
explanation: Articaine has a thiophene ring with an ester group that plasma esterases hydrolyze quickly, giving it a short elimination half-life.

question: Ibuprofen relieves dental pain by:
explanation: Ibuprofen is a reversible, nonselective cyclooxygenase inhibitor that cuts prostaglandin formation. Aspirin is the drug that acetylates COX irreversibly.

question: For an adult with acute dental pain and no contraindications, which approach does current evidence-based guidance favor first?
explanation: ADA guidance for acute dental pain recommends NSAIDs, alone or with acetaminophen, as first-line care and opioids only when these are not enough or cannot be used.

question: The main danger of an acetaminophen overdose is:
explanation: Excess acetaminophen saturates normal pathways and forms the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which depletes glutathione and injures liver cells; acetylcysteine is the antidote.

question: Which drug reverses respiratory depression from an opioid?
explanation: Naloxone competitively blocks opioid receptors. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; naloxone may need repeating because its action can be shorter than the opioid's.

question: A patient on warfarin is prescribed metronidazole. What is the likely result?
explanation: Metronidazole inhibits warfarin metabolism (CYP2C9), so warfarin levels and the INR rise and bleeding risk increases; another antibiotic or INR monitoring is needed.

question: What does clavulanic acid add when combined with amoxicillin?
optionA: It slows renal excretion of amoxicillin
explanation: Clavulanate binds and inactivates beta-lactamases, protecting amoxicillin from bacteria that would otherwise destroy it.

question: Clarithromycin can raise blood levels of simvastatin and cause muscle injury because it:
explanation: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, so drugs cleared by CYP3A4, such as simvastatin, build up; azithromycin has far less of this effect.

question: Which oral diabetes drug works mainly by lowering glucose output from the liver?
explanation: Metformin, a biguanide, suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis and rarely causes hypoglycemia on its own. Sulfonylureas such as glipizide raise insulin release and can cause hypoglycemia.

question: Pilocarpine helps some patients with dry mouth because it is a:
explanation: Pilocarpine stimulates muscarinic receptors on remaining salivary tissue, increasing flow; sweating is a common side effect, and it needs some working gland to act on.

question: Midazolam produces sedation by:
explanation: Benzodiazepines increase how often the GABA-A chloride channel opens, enhancing inhibition. Ketamine blocks NMDA receptors.

question: Case: 52-year-old man on propranolol for hypertension receives several cartridges with epinephrine. What reaction is most likely?
optionA: Fall in blood pressure, fast pulse
optionD: Rise in blood pressure, slow pulse
explanation: With beta receptors blocked by a nonselective beta-blocker, epinephrine acts mainly on alpha receptors, raising blood pressure and causing reflex bradycardia, so epinephrine is limited.

question: Case: 61-year-old woman with a prosthetic aortic valve and a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin needs scaling. Which oral premedication is appropriate?
explanation: Cephalosporins should not be used after anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria with penicillins, and the 2021 AHA statement no longer recommends clindamycin; azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline are options.

question: Case: 47-year-old man who needs premedication for endocarditis is already taking amoxicillin for a sinus infection. What should be given before his periodontal surgery?
optionD: A double dose the night before
explanation: When the patient is already on an antibiotic, guidance is to choose a drug of a different class, such as azithromycin or clarithromycin, rather than more of the same.

question: Case: 66-year-old woman who needs endocarditis prophylaxis forgot to take it before an extraction that has just started. What is acceptable?
optionA: Cancel and reschedule for next week
optionC: Give it up to 2 hours after
explanation: The dose is meant before the procedure, but if it was not taken it may be given up to 2 hours after the procedure.

question: Case: 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on apixaban needs one simple extraction. What is the usual approach?
optionA: Stop it 7 days before the extraction
optionC: Give vitamin K the day before
explanation: For a minor procedure with low bleeding risk, the anticoagulant is usually continued and bleeding controlled locally; any interruption is decided with the prescriber, and vitamin K does not reverse apixaban.

question: A general dentist sends a patient with a calcified, curved molar canal to an endodontist rather than attempt it. Under the ADA Code, this mainly reflects:
explanation: The ADA Code places consultation and referral under nonmaleficence (do no harm): dentists seek help from those with special skills when it protects the patient.

question: When an endodontist finishes treating a referred patient, what does the ADA Code expect, unless the patient asks otherwise?
optionA: Keep the patient for all future care
optionB: Return the patient to the referrer
optionC: Send the patient to a new general dentist
optionD: Discharge the patient with no referral
explanation: Under the Code, specialists and consultants return the patient to the referring dentist, or to the dentist of record, unless the patient expressly prefers otherwise.

question: A dentist accepts an insurer's payment as payment in full and quietly never collects the patient's copayment. Under the ADA Code, this is:
optionB: Acceptable if the patient is poor
explanation: The Code calls this overbilling: the claim makes the charge look higher than it really is, which is deception under the principle of veracity, unless the waiver is disclosed to the third party.

question: A dentist stops treating a patient halfway through a bridge after a dispute, without notice. Under the ADA Code, this is:
explanation: Once treatment has begun, the dentist should not stop without adequate notice and a chance for the patient to find another dentist, and the patient's oral health must not be put at risk.

question: A dentist knows first-hand that a colleague is treating patients while impaired by alcohol. Under the ADA Code, what is expected?
optionA: Urge treatment and report the evidence
optionB: Say nothing unless a patient complains
optionC: Report only after a second incident occurs
optionD: Report him to the police at once
explanation: The Code obliges dentists to urge impaired colleagues to seek treatment and to report first-hand evidence to the professional assistance committee of a dental society.

question: A dentist recommends removing sound amalgam fillings from a non-allergic patient to rid the body of toxins. Under the ADA Code, this is:
optionD: A matter of patient autonomy alone
explanation: The Code states that removing amalgam from a non-allergic patient for the alleged purpose of removing toxins, on the dentist's own recommendation, is improper and unethical under veracity.

question: A new patient's existing restorations are poorly done. Under the ADA Code's view of justifiable criticism, what should the dentist do?
optionA: Tell the patient the last dentist was negligent
optionD: Report the last dentist to the board at once
explanation: Patients should be told the facts of their current oral health without disparaging comment about prior work, and consulting the previous dentist is encouraged; only gross or continual faulty treatment is reported.

question: Which element must be part of valid informed consent for an extraction?
optionA: The fee schedule of the office
explanation: Informed consent means the patient understands the diagnosis, the proposed treatment, its risks and benefits and the reasonable alternatives, including no treatment.

question: A dental practice bills insurers electronically. A billing company processes those claims for it. Under HIPAA, the billing company is a:
explanation: A business associate performs functions involving protected health information on behalf of a covered entity and must sign a business associate agreement; the practice that transmits claims electronically is the covered entity.

question: Under HIPAA, a patient who asks for a copy of her own record must generally receive it within:
explanation: The right of access requires action within 30 days of the request, with one 30-day extension allowed if the patient is told why in writing.

question: A laptop with unencrypted records of 120 patients is stolen. Under the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule, the patients must be told:
optionB: Only if the press reports it
explanation: Individuals must be notified without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery. Breaches of fewer than 500 people are also logged and reported to HHS each year.

question: A patient's benefits year has just reset, and she asks the dentist to date last month's crown as this month so the plan pays. Under the ADA Code, doing so is:
optionB: Allowed if the fee is unchanged
optionD: A false representation to the plan
explanation: Reporting incorrect treatment dates to help a patient get benefits that would otherwise be disallowed is an unethical, false or misleading representation under the Code's veracity section.

question: A dentist praises a 5-year-old at once each time she keeps her mouth open. Which behavior principle is being used?
explanation: Adding something pleasant right after a behavior makes it more likely to happen again. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant, and extinction withholds reinforcement.

question: A dentist helps a fearful adult relax while gradually facing more anxiety-provoking steps, from sitting in the chair to an injection. This is:
explanation: Systematic desensitization pairs relaxation with a graded hierarchy of feared stimuli, so each step is tolerated before moving on.

question: Under Piaget's stages, a typical 4-year-old who thinks the drill is angry at him is in which stage?
explanation: Children of about 2 to 7 years are preoperational: egocentric, magical thinking and giving life to objects, so simple, concrete words work best.

question: A Spanish-speaking patient brings her 10-year-old son to interpret for a discussion of oral surgery. What is best?
optionC: Ask the front-desk clerk to translate
explanation: Children should not interpret clinical information: they may lack vocabulary, omit details and face a burden. A trained interpreter supports valid informed consent.

question: Case: 81-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer's disease needs extractions. Her daughter holds her durable power of attorney for health care. Who gives consent?
optionA: The daughter, as her legal representative
optionB: The patient alone, because she is present
optionC: The dentist, acting in her best interest
optionD: Any family member who comes along
explanation: When a patient lacks capacity, the person legally authorized, here the health care agent, gives consent, while the patient is still involved as far as she is able.

question: Case: 34-year-old man with HIV, well controlled on therapy, asks for routine fillings. The dentist feels uneasy. Under the ADA Code, what is required?
optionA: Refer him to an HIV dental clinic
optionB: Treat him as any other patient
optionC: Treat him only at day's end
optionD: Ask for his viral load in writing
explanation: The Code holds that a dentist may not refuse a patient because of a bloodborne infection; decisions on treatment or referral are made on the same basis as for any patient, and standard precautions apply to all.

question: Case: 7-year-old girl with untreated decay in many teeth and a facial abscess; the parent has missed several appointments despite reminders and free transport. What is the dentist's duty?
optionA: Wait for the parent to call back
optionB: Report it if she misses one more visit
optionD: Close the chart and discharge her
explanation: Willful failure to get needed care for a child, after the parent understands the problem and barriers have been addressed, can be dental neglect, and the ADA Code obliges dentists to report suspected neglect under state law.

question: Case: A patient calls on Saturday with severe pain and swelling after a root canal begun two days ago. Under the ADA Code, the dentist must:
optionA: Tell him to wait until Monday
optionB: Refer him to an endodontist next week
optionC: Charge first, then decide to help
explanation: Dentists are obliged to make reasonable arrangements for emergency care of their patients of record, whether by seeing them or arranging coverage.

question: What is the main purpose of randomly assigning patients to treatment groups in a trial?
explanation: Randomization spreads known and unknown confounders evenly between groups, so differences in outcome can be attributed to the treatment.

question: Which measure of association is calculated in a case-control study?
explanation: A case-control study starts from outcome, so it cannot measure incidence; it compares the odds of exposure in cases and controls, giving an odds ratio.

question: A cross-sectional survey of a town's adults mainly measures:
explanation: A cross-sectional study takes one snapshot of exposure and disease, so it gives prevalence but cannot show which came first.

question: A caries detection device is used on 200 people who are caries-free; 180 test negative. What is its specificity?
explanation: Specificity is true negatives divided by all people without disease: 180 / 200 = 90%. The 20 false positives give a false-positive rate of 10%.

question: If a screening test is used in a population where the disease becomes much rarer, its positive predictive value will:
explanation: Predictive values depend on prevalence: with fewer true cases, a larger share of positive results are false positives, so PPV drops while sensitivity and specificity stay the same.

question: A trial finds no difference between two sealants when a real difference exists. This is a:
explanation: A type II error (beta) is failing to reject a false null hypothesis, missing a real effect, often because the sample is too small. A type I error finds a difference that is not real.

question: Which change most directly increases a study's statistical power?
explanation: Power rises with sample size, effect size and alpha, and falls with greater variability; enlarging the sample is the usual way to raise it.

question: A study reports a relative risk of 1.4 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.9 to 2.1. What can be concluded?
explanation: Because the interval includes 1.0, no difference in risk, the result is not significant at the 5% level.

question: In a trial, 20% of control children and 10% of treated children develop new caries. What is the number needed to treat?
explanation: The absolute risk reduction is 20% minus 10% = 10%, or 0.10, and the number needed to treat is 1 / 0.10 = 10.

question: Which measure of central tendency best describes a skewed distribution such as household income?
explanation: Extreme values pull the mean toward the tail, while the median, the middle value, is resistant to them. Range and standard deviation measure spread, not center.

question: In a normal distribution, about what share of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean?
explanation: About 68% lie within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD and 99.7% within 3 SD of the mean.

question: Why are both patients and examiners kept unaware of group assignment in a double-blind trial?
optionC: To remove the need for consent
explanation: Blinding stops expectations from shaping how participants report and how examiners score outcomes; it does not replace consent.

question: In a PICO question, what does the letter I stand for?
explanation: PICO is Patient or problem, Intervention, Comparison and Outcome, the frame for an answerable clinical question.

question: Which statistic measures agreement between two examiners beyond what chance alone would give?
explanation: Kappa corrects raw percent agreement for chance agreement, so it is used to calibrate examiners scoring categories such as caries codes. Pearson's r measures linear correlation.

question: Which test compares the proportions of patients with caries in two groups?
explanation: Counts of categories (caries yes or no by group) are compared with the chi-square test. A t-test compares means of continuous data.

question: Which standard code set describes the procedures a dentist performs, for records and claims?
explanation: The Code on Dental Procedures and Nomenclature (CDT) describes procedures. ICD-10-CM codes and SNODENT describe diagnoses and findings, and NDC numbers identify drugs.

question: In a trial analyzed by intention to treat, patients are counted:
optionB: Only if they finished the treatment
optionC: In the group they ended up in
optionD: Only if they had no side effects
explanation: Intention-to-treat analysis keeps patients in their assigned groups whatever happened later, which preserves the benefit of randomization.

question: Case: A dentist reads a trial of a new varnish. Of 100 children in each group, 40% of the treated group dropped out, mostly those with new lesions. Which problem threatens the result?
explanation: When those who drop out differ in outcome, the remaining groups are no longer comparable and the effect can look larger than it is.

question: Case: A practice wants fewer failed appointments. It tries text reminders for one month, checks the no-show rate and then expands the change. Which quality model is this?
explanation: PDSA tests a small change, studies the data, then adopts, adapts or abandons it in repeated cycles of improvement.

question: Case: Researchers ask adults with and without oral cancer how much they smoked 20 years ago. People with cancer recall more exposure. What bias is this?
explanation: Case-control studies ask about past exposure, and cases often search their memories harder than controls, inflating the association.
